DOCUMENT:
"""
Categorising invoices into the correct General Ledger (GL) code is critical for accurate financial reporting and tax compliance, yet this remains a complex task due to the diversity in organizational accounting practices—what we refer to as “unique accounting contexts.” In our dataset, these contexts manifested as, for example, varying vendor-specific GL code assignments (e.g., stationery purchases coded as office expenses for one client but as administrative overhead for another), custom and nested GL hierarchies, and divergent invoice description conventions (such as local jargon or acronyms). Practically, some companies grouped employee expenses under a catch-all code, while others maintained fine-grained codes for each expense category. These idiosyncrasies required careful operationalisation, which meant collecting metadata about each organization’s chart of accounts and coding policies and encoding these business rules into the dataset where applicable.

Standard AI solutions, often designed for broader, less variable domains, may struggle to adapt to such idiosyncrasies, resulting in reduced accuracy or opaque error modes. Our study addresses these challenges for businesses seeking reliable, interpretable automation within their own defined financial operations.

Specifically, we investigate whether small in-house language models (SLMs) can offer competitive accuracy, enhanced data security, and improved interpretability versus larger, cloud-based models. Prior work [1,2] highlights the limitations of general-purpose models—including dependence on external APIs, exposure risks, and weak handling of domain-specific terms—and underscores the need for tailored solutions.

We evaluated two pre-trained transformer models—SBERT (Sentence-BERT, a sentence transformer) and DeBERTa (a classic small language model)—by fine-tuning both on a proprietary financial text corpus. Our dataset comprised 10,000 labeled invoices from mid-sized companies in manufacturing, consulting, and logistics, spanning 45 GL codes (class frequencies ranged from 3000 invoices for the most common code to 30 for the rarest, with the top 10 codes covering 60% of labels), over 300 vendors, and varied invoice formats. Annotation involved a two-stage process: initial pre-labeling by accounting software where possible, followed by manual review by professional accountants. Ambiguous cases were independently coded by two annotators, with Cohen’s kappa averaging 0.83 on a 500-sample subset, and adjudication used for any disagreement. Disagreements and invoices with incomplete vendor histories were flagged and, where possible, resolved through consensus discussion.

All invoices were de-identified and split into structured fields (e.g., vendor name, invoice date, line items, total, and description) and raw OCR text for model input. For structured variants, only fields consistently present and reliably extracted across invoices were used; missing or ambiguous fields were imputed as blank tokens or excluded from feature construction. Data preprocessing additionally included lower-casing, tokenization, duplicate removal, and conversion of numerical fields to standardized string representations to reduce sparsity.

We reserved 10% of the data (1,000 invoices) as a held-out test set, selected by stratified sampling across GL codes and vendors to ensure diversity and maintain class proportions. Model hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs) were optimized for each model independently using 5-fold cross-validation on the remaining training data. Both SBERT and DeBERTa were fine-tuned for classification using identical training protocols, which entailed the AdamW optimizer, a batch size of 32, early stopping with patience of 3 epochs based on validation loss, and a maximum of 10 epochs per run. Internal train/validation splits (90/10) were consistent across experiments for comparability.

For baselines, we implemented: (a) a zero-shot LLM using GPT-3 via API, prompted as follows: “Assign the following invoice text to the most appropriate GL code from this list: [GL codes]. Invoice: [invoice text].” Multiple prompt formulations were tested, varying context descriptions and explicitness of GL code options; however, F1 varied by ≤0.02 across versions, so the best-performing prompt was used for reporting. (b) a vendor-based rule assigning the most frequent GL code previously observed for each vendor in the training set. This baseline is motivated by industry practice, where vendor history often serves as a fallback when automation is absent; it provides a plausible non-ML comparator and sets a floor for machine performance.

On the held-out test set, SBERT achieved 0.96 accuracy and 0.93 average F1 score; DeBERTa reached 0.93 accuracy and 0.89 F1, while the zero-shot LLM resulted in 0.83 accuracy and 0.81 F1. The vendor-based baseline achieved 0.74 accuracy and 0.68 F1. Macro-F1 scores were 0.84 for SBERT, 0.81 for DeBERTa, 0.69 for the LLM, and 0.49 for the vendor-based rule. The lowest per-class F1 for SBERT was 0.37 (for the rarest code), while the most common classes exceeded 0.97. Supplementary Table 1 details full per-class F1 and precision/recall values. To assess statistical robustness, we computed 95% confidence intervals via bootstrapping (e.g., SBERT accuracy: [0.957, 0.965]; DeBERTa: [0.922, 0.937]), confirming observed differences were significant for SLMs versus baselines. Both SLMs performed robustly when generalizing to new clients (e.g., SBERT yielded 0.90 F1 after training with ~100 client-specific invoices) and consistently outperformed baselines for infrequent GL codes, though class imbalance (some GL codes received <1% of labels) did affect overall sensitivity.

To mitigate class imbalance, we primarily relied on stratified sampling in train/test splits to preserve rare classes, and incorporated class weighting in the loss function during model training. Oversampling of rare classes was piloted, but led to modest (≤0.01) increases in rare-class F1 at the expense of greater overfitting and instability in validation metrics, so was not adopted in the final protocol.

To better understand embedding behaviors and inform interpretability, we quantitatively measured cluster properties. Sentence embeddings were “globally anisotropic but locally isotropic”—i.e., overall embedding space is uneven (as per [3]), while invoices from a single vendor cluster compactly. Silhouette scores (mean: 0.52) and intra- versus inter-cluster Euclidean distances (intra: 0.39±0.05, inter: 1.12±0.22, normalized units) matched qualitative observations: denser embedding clusters correlated with higher classification accuracy for well-represented classes and vendors; for rare GL codes, looser clusters aligned with reduced F1. Principal component projections confirmed vendor identity as a dominant but imperfect signal—clusters by GL code, especially for underrepresented codes, were more diffuse, which explained much of the error pattern for imbalanced classes. This analysis guided calibration of the models, including the decision to aggregate over multiple random initializations to minimize arbitrary embedding drift.

Interpretability and auditability were explored by visualizing attention maps and intermediate activations for representative invoices; for instance, we observed that SBERT’s attention focused on line item descriptions and vendor metadata for the majority of prediction steps. Invoices with ambiguous or atypical language (or from new vendors) triggered more diffuse attention patterns and—upon audit—proved more likely to be misclassified. These findings helped inform our guidance for model users and further support trust in model predictions. All visualization summaries are provided in Supplementary Figure 2; key examples are discussed in the supplement.

Contrary to previous claims [4], formatting invoices into structured fields (including line items, totals, and vendor metadata) did not significantly improve SLM performance over plain OCR text (ΔF1 <0.01), suggesting key patterns are efficiently extracted from unstructured input. Missing or systematically ambiguous fields were found to have negligible impact on overall results.

Our study has several limitations. First, moderate dataset size and focus on the manufacturing, consulting, and logistics sectors may constrain generalizability to very different accounting regimes or highly novel invoice formats. Second, despite multi-level annotation and validation, label noise may persist: ambiguous invoices, human error during manual coding, or incomplete vendor histories can all introduce inaccuracies, partially mitigated by consensus coding and flagging outliers for review. Third, class imbalance among GL codes, with some classes rarely observed, remains a source of reduced performance for minority codes despite stratified sampling and class weighting.

Finally, while SLMs offer advantages in data security (all processing in-house), interpretability (intermediate activations can be visualized and audited as described above), and transparency, these gains come with operational costs. Deploying and maintaining SLM infrastructure requires ongoing updates to account for evolving accounting standards, drift in invoice formats, and periodic re-training for new vendors or business lines—necessitating dedicated staff and tooling. Fully managed LLM solutions, while less firm-specific, offer greater ease of scaling but at the expense of customization and control.

In summary, and consistent with prior research [1,2], our results demonstrate that small, fine-tuned in-house SLMs can outperform both off-the-shelf LLMs and simple heuristics for invoice categorisation, delivering a practical and more secure alternative for organizations seeking tailored, auditable AI-driven accounting automation.

References:  
[1] M. Huber et al., "Domain-Specific Language Models for Financial Document Classification," J. of Accounting Analytics, 2022.  
[2] L. Sun et al., "Improving Invoice Automation with Custom NLP Models," Proc. ACL Finance Workshop, 2023.  
[3] Y. Ethayarajh, "How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations? Comparing the Geometry of BERT, ELMo
